label: Lost the story
title: Hatshepsut Didn’t Pretend to Be a Man. She Dressed as a King, and Egypt Couldn’t Stand It.
dek: Pop history files her under “cross-dressers.” Her own statues file her under “she.” Every king wore a fake beard. Hers is the only one anyone calls a disguise.
summary: Hatshepsut’s statues moved from queen to bearded king while their grammar kept calling her ‘she’; who recarved her, who erased her and why.

blocks.text: THE WARDROBE: Every Egyptian king wore a fake beard. It tied on with a strap. Hers is the only one anyone calls a disguise. (Tag: False beard. One size fits all pharaohs.)

Egyptian kings were generally clean-shaven. The beard on their statues was a false one, strapped on as a badge of office, and on one Met statue of Hatshepsut you can see the strap. So she wasn’t putting on a man’s beard. She was putting on the king’s. Even on her bearded statues, the inscriptions kept calling her “she.” Her personal name means “Foremost of Noble Ladies,” and it was never made masculine. Everyone knew exactly who was wearing the crown. At least twenty years after she died, someone decided that was the problem.
A woman in three chairs

You probably know her as the pharaoh who was secretly a woman. Listverse put her on a 2013 list of historical cross-dressers. A March 2026 NPR illustrated piece said she was among the first people known to change their gender.
The older story is meaner: a scheming stepmother steals the throne from a boy king, who grows up and smashes her statues.

Walk into the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and sit with three of her statues. First, a woman’s sheath dress. Second, the same dress under a king’s striped headcloth. Third, the king’s kilt on a body the Met still reads as feminine. Her titles on the thrones carry feminine endings.
A costume change, done in public, with the name tag left on.
c. 1785 BCE: Somebody else wore the kilt first
About 300 years earlier, a woman named Sobekneferu ruled Egypt as king for almost four years.

A headless statue of her (Louvre E 27135) shows a dress, a king’s kilt and the nemes, the striped royal headcloth. Kelly-Anne Diamond, an Egyptologist at Villanova, argues the mix was modeled on creator gods.
So Hatshepsut did not invent the look. But Sobekneferu stopped at the layered outfit. Hatshepsut kept going until the dress was gone.
Her temple at Deir el-Bahri, where the paperwork was carved in stone: a divine birth, a father’s blessing, a god’s pick. Photo: Diego Delso (cropped), CC BY-SA 4.0
c. 1479 BCE: The queen in the dress

Hatshepsut was the daughter of the pharaoh Thutmose I and the wife of the next one, Thutmose II. When he died, the heir was a small boy, Thutmose III, son of a lesser wife. Hatshepsut became his regent.
At first, the pictures followed the rules. A temple at Semna, in Nubia, names one king in year 2: the boy. Hatshepsut stands to the side as queen.
Her rank came from a priestly office as well: God’s Wife of Amun, a powerful title held by royal women. The pictures still showed a queen.
For now, the boy got the crown and she got the dress.
Year 7 (c. 1473 BCE): The queen tries on the crown
The best clue to her crowning is a wine jar.

The tomb of the parents of Senenmut, her steward and overseer of works, held a jar dated to year 7. Next to it were seals with her queen’s title and seals with her new king’s name, Maatkare. Old business card, new business card, same drawer.

Most specialists put the crowning late in year 7. Some scholars argue for year 2. A coronation text quoted by Dimitri Laboury, a Belgian Egyptologist, describes it in terms of regalia: “she wore the insignias of Ra.”

Her first king images kept the woman in view. A Luxor fragment puts a king’s crown over female clothes. The Met’s seated statue 30.3.3 pairs a sheath dress with the khat headcloth. On a Karnak block described by Peter Dorman, a University of Chicago Egyptologist, she offers wine to Amun, a rite reserved for kings, under a king’s crown and title, in a gown down to her ankles.
King’s work. Queen’s clothes.
Her temple at Deir el-Bahri supplied the paperwork. Dorman counts three scenes:

rows: The god Amun visits her mother in the form of Thutmose I. The child is called “daughter.” A later king, Amenhotep III, carved nearly the same story.¹
Thutmose I names her his heir. No independent evidence backs it. Specialists treat it as written later.
Amun picks her out as the future king.

blocks.text: No text names a designer. Senenmut is only a guess. The fair answer is a court circle: Senenmut, the priests of Amun and Hatshepsut herself.
The boy stayed in the picture, crowned but usually standing behind her. Dorman says calling her rise a usurpation is “hardly accurate.”
No grab. A paper trail, in stone.
After year 7: Her own sculptors recarve the gown
Once she was king, the image moved one way only.

In 1979, the scholar Roland Tefnin showed her statues follow a “progressive and irreversible masculinization.” Laboury finds the same in her wall carvings. The order is reconstructed. The direction is not in doubt.
Then her artists edited their own work. At Buhen, in Nubia, her king figures were first carved striding in a woman’s long gown. Laboury reports they were later recut as men.

blocks.title: The costume change, in four statues

blocks.text: The Met’s seated and kneeling statues, in the order scholars reconstruct. Watch the outfit change. Watch the grammar not change.

rows: The grammar says SHE: Full king’s titles
The grammar says SHE: “Lady of the Two Lands”
King’s kilt on a body the Met reads as feminine. No beard.
The grammar says SHE: Feminine titles
Male king’s body, false beard. On 29.3.1 you can see the strap.
The grammar says SHE: Still a feminine form

blocks.text: Statues: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Rogers Fund, 1929–30. Public domain. 29.3.3 includes a torso on loan from Leiden.
The Met’s kneeling Hatshepsut. Look along the jaw: the king’s beard is tied on with a strap. Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 29.3.1, public domain.
The paint changed too. Egyptian art painted women yellow and men reddish-brown. Her temple’s sphinxes, lion bodies with her face, were painted yellow.
Swatches approximate. Built by SIDE EYE.

In her sanctuary, her skin went from a pinkish in-between shade to dark red, probably while she was alive. A Karnak block still holds yellow paint inside her reworked face. Laboury reads that as a sign the makeover began on her side.
The first people to recarve Hatshepsut probably worked for Hatshepsut.
c. 1473–1458 BCE: The beard goes on. The grammar stays.
The finished look is the museum poster: a young, bare-chested king with a false beard. On the Met’s kneeling statue 29.3.1, you can see the beard’s strap along her face.

Did she wear one in person? Nobody knows. Every bearded Hatshepsut is a statue or carving. Laboury has no doubt she appeared in public dressed as a female pharaoh. In his view, the male image showed “what was meant, instead of what really was.”
The writing never played along. “Son of Re” became “Daughter of Re.” Her personal name stayed feminine. Even the bearded kneeling statue 30.3.2 still uses a feminine form.
Cathleen Keller, a Berkeley Egyptologist, told Smithsonian in 2006: “She was not pretending to be a man!”
The beard said “king.” The grammar said “her.”
c. 1458 BCE and after: The chisels wait, then edit out the king
Hatshepsut died around 1458 BCE. Thutmose III ruled alone for about three more decades.

If he hated her, he took his time. Dorman dates the campaign by a Karnak hall, built no earlier than his year 42, that walled in her reliefs mid-erasure. Even so, that is at least twenty years after her death.

One wrinkle. Kara Cooney, an Egyptologist, writes that some giant Karnak statues of her were renamed in year 2 of his sole reign. She is our only source for that, and we could not trace it to a primary record.
When the stonecutters came, they edited. Peter Brand, an Egyptologist, says her names were often recut as Thutmose I or II, less often Thutmose III. On paper, the kingship now ran man to man.

At Medinet Habu, her figure was cut away and replaced with a table of offerings.² Through later paint and plaster, traces of her original figures can still be seen. The royal cobra on her statues’ brows was usually chiseled off.

Emily Teeter, an Egyptologist reviewing the Met’s 2005 catalogue, reports that the changes hit “only those that showed her as king.” Cooney says scenes of her as queen supporting her husband were left alone. No full count exists. Treat it as strong specialist reading, not a census.

Why? Dorman sees a response to her unusual public image, not necessarily a personal attack. Other scholars suggest Thutmose III was securing the throne for his son, Amenhotep II, though no rival claimant is known.
By the best specialist account, they did not erase the woman. They erased the king she had become.
1829 to 2026: The captions outlive the chisel
In 1829, Jean-François Champollion, the French scholar who first read hieroglyphs, toured her temple. He found a bearded king surrounded by feminine grammar. He was puzzled, not scandalized.

rows: Sobekneferu rules as king in a kilt over a dress.
Thutmose II dies. Hatshepsut becomes regent for a little boy.
She’s crowned king. The dress starts coming off, statue by statue.
She dies. Thutmose III rules alone.
At least 20 years later, the chisels edit out the king.
Champollion finds a bearded king who is a “she.” Puzzled, not scandalized.
The Met finds her smashed statues and invents a villain.
Ritual “deactivation,” says one study. A woman’s work destroyed, says the reply.

blocks.text: She survived on paper, too. Manetho, an Egyptian priest writing in Greek more than a thousand years later, still recorded a woman ruler.

The villain came later, from the museum that dug her up. In the 1920s, the Met excavator Herbert Winlock found pits of her broken statues and read them as Thutmose’s spite. Met curator William C. Hayes called her “vain, ambitious, and unscrupulous.”
In 2005–06, the same museum’s exhibition rehabilitated her. Same statues, new captions.

rows: ~~”Vain, ambitious, and unscrupulous.”~~ Curator William C. Hayes

blocks.text: In 2025, Jun Yi Wong, a Toronto Egyptologist, reexamined Winlock’s records in Antiquity. Male kings’ statues at the site were broken in comparable ways. He reads it as ritual “deactivation,” switching a statue off, plus later reuse as raw material. Headlines said gender was not the main factor. His paper does not analyze gender at all.
In May 2026, Cooney answered on Substack. The breakage, she wrote, is “systematic destruction of a woman’s political body of work.”
The argument is open. The villain is retired.
The outfit was the argument

Her own workshops carved her into the one body Egyptian art gave a king. At least twenty years after her death, by the best specialist reading, the state cut the king back out and recut her names as her father’s and husband’s.
At Medinet Habu, a table of food covers the spot where she stood. Traces of her still show through the plaster.

blocks.title: What we can prove / what we can’t

blocks.text: Proven:

items: Her image moved from queen to female king to male king, gradually, mostly after year 7.
Her inscriptions kept feminine grammar, even on bearded statues.
The king’s beard was a tied-on fake. Kings were generally clean-shaven.
Sobekneferu wore a king’s kilt over a dress centuries earlier.
The main erasure campaign began no earlier than Thutmose III’s year 42, at least twenty years after her death.

blocks.text: Strongly supported:

items: Her own workshops recarved and repainted her as male, probably during her reign (Laboury).
Her claim rested on planned scenes: divine birth, presentation by her father, an oracle (Dorman).
The “vain, ambitious” Hatshepsut was largely a 20th-century creation.

blocks.text: Likely:

items: The erasure targeted her as king and generally spared her as queen (Teeter; Cooney).
The motive mixed succession and an all-male record, with gender part of it.

blocks.text: Not proven:

items: That she wore a beard or male clothes in person.
That Senenmut designed her image, or was her lover.
That her father really crowned her.
That the erasure was revenge or simple misogyny. Wong’s study does not address gender. The early renaming rests on Cooney alone.
That the mummy identified in 2007 is hers.

blocks.text: The other side

In Egyptian art, “king” was one picture: young, male, kilted, bearded. So the male body defined the office, not her sex. The Egyptologist Uroš Matić argues “cross-dresser” forces a modern idea of gender onto that kingship. Keller, Laboury and the Met agree. They are right about the disguise. But the male body was still a choice, made in steps by her own workshops. That is why “rebrand” survives and “disguise” does not.
Why the gap?

Maybe Thutmose III wanted a clean father-to-son record, and a woman king did not fit. Maybe a woman in the king’s body was the problem. To the Egyptians, those may have been one problem. The stone shows what they removed. The grammar they missed still says “she.”
The beard said “King.” The grammar said “Her.”
¹ [H.C.] I would like it noted that the god Amun visited her mother disguised as her father. If anyone in this story wore a disguise, it was the god.
² [H.C.] They swapped a pharaoh for a table of food. I am choosing to find that comforting.

blocks.title: SIDE EYE · Sidebar: The pharaoh dress code

blocks.text: Kingship attire policy, Egypt, c. 1473–1458 BCE. Subject to change by chisel.

items: Beards. Kings are generally clean-shaven. The office supplies a fake one. Straps may show.
Kilts. Not a new look. Sobekneferu wore one over a dress about 300 years earlier.
Skin. Women yellow, men reddish-brown. Switching? Paint over the yellow. It may show through.
Off duty. Beard compliance in person: unknown. Every bearded Hatshepsut on file is a statue or carving.
Enforcement. Begins no earlier than Thutmose III’s year 42. Names may be recut as your father’s or husband’s.

blocks.text: Queen attire: generally exempt, per the best specialist reading.
